strengths: GIQ targets a meaningful gap: evaluating geometric properties using well-defined polyhedra rather than heterogeneous everyday objects. Pairing synthetic renderings with physical paper models is a useful and labor-intensive contribution.
The benchmark covers diverse convex, nonconvex, stellated, and compound shapes, supporting several complementary tasks and controlled studies of synthetic-to-real transfer.

The symmetry experiment provides promising quantitative evidence: it uses balanced accuracy, excludes training shapes from the test set, and compares nine featurizers. DINOv2 reaches 0.93 balanced accuracy for four-fold symmetry on real images after training on synthetic images.
weaknesses: The mental-rotation evaluation does not substantiate its central chance-level conclusion. Figure 2 explicitly reports accuracy only on negative pairs, which measures specificity rather than overall discrimination; an always-negative classifier would score 100%. Positive-pair performance, balanced accuracy, threshold selection, and full confusion matrices are needed. The hard-split construction and potential image or shape overlap are also insufficiently specified.

Reconstruction evidence is limited to qualitative comparisons of three selected shapes under synthetic and real conditions. There are no aggregate geometric metrics, uncertainty estimates, or systematic analyses against shape complexity. These examples illustrate failures but cannot support broad claims about reconstruction capabilities across the dataset.

The tasks do not adequately isolate geometric reasoning. Naming obscure polyhedra also requires specialized lexical knowledge, while synthetic-to-real matching changes color, background, lighting, and appearance alongside viewpoint. Property-based questions, controlled appearance and rotation ablations, and human performance would help distinguish geometric limitations from naming difficulty, domain shift, and single-view ambiguity.

Reproducibility is insufficient in the supplied manuscript. Important split details and additional results are deferred to supplementary material that is not included. Exact encoder checkpoints, feature extraction and probe-training settings, hard-pair sample counts, and VLM versions, inference settings, image sampling, and answer-adjudication rules are missing. A Gemini example claims web-search use, but tool-access conditions are not explained.

The symmetry results are encouraging but lack confidence intervals, repeated splits, and controls for category or silhouette shortcuts. With only 26 held-out shapes, many correlated views do not establish broad geometric generalization. Excluding all Johnson solids because of viewing ambiguities further narrows the evidence, and linear decodability alone does not establish explicit 3D reasoning.

Dataset documentation needs greater precision. Table 1 lists overlapping categories without explaining their reconciliation to 224 unique shapes, and the relationship between synthetic coverage and the physical subset is unclear. There are also mathematical inaccuracies: Archimedean solids are not generally edge-transitive, and Catalan solids generally have face transitivity rather than vertex uniformity. Such issues matter for a benchmark whose principal value is precise geometric ground truth.

strengths: The collection of synthetic renderings and hand-built physical polyhedra is a distinctive, potentially useful resource. Controlled geometry and varied real-world photographs could support detailed studies of geometric perception and domain shift.
The paper evaluates a broad range of models across four complementary tasks, including nine visual encoders, three reconstruction methods, and four frontier VLMs.

The symmetry experiment uses balanced accuracy and holds out 26 shapes rather than merely unseen views. DINOv2’s reported synthetic-to-real performance, including 0.93 balanced accuracy for four-fold symmetry, is a promising empirical result.
weaknesses: The mental-rotation conclusion has a major metric problem. Figure 2 explicitly reports accuracy on negative pairs alone, which measures specificity rather than overall discrimination. An always-different classifier would score 100% on this subset. Without positive-pair results, balanced accuracy, or threshold-independent metrics, values near 50% do not establish chance-level task performance.

Reconstruction evidence is limited to qualitative results for three selected shapes, each with synthetic and real inputs. No dataset-wide geometric metrics, uncertainty estimates, or systematic complexity analysis are reported. These examples illustrate failures but cannot substantiate broad claims about reconstruction capabilities across the benchmark.

The experiments do not adequately isolate geometric reasoning. Synthetic-to-real matching changes color, material, lighting, and background alongside viewpoint; linear-probe limitations need not imply limitations of the underlying representations. Exact polyhedron naming also depends on specialized vocabulary and factual knowledge. Controlled appearance ablations, direct geometric-property questions, and stronger task-specific baselines would help distinguish these explanations.

Benchmark composition and reproducibility are insufficiently documented. Table 1’s category counts sum to 238 rather than 224; overlapping categories could explain this, but their membership is not reconciled. Figure 1 describes 224 real polyhedra, whereas Section 3.4 includes only 48 of the 92 Johnson solids. Exact image counts, shape inventories, hard-pair splits, model checkpoints, probe hyperparameters, and statistical uncertainty are missing from the supplied manuscript. Referenced supplementary material is not included, and the advertised dataset link has no accessible target in the PDF.

The VLM evaluation omits sample counts, view aggregation, acceptable naming variants, grading procedures, repeated trials, and precise inference settings. One Gemini example claims to use Google search, leaving tool access and comparability unclear. Four selected explanations do not establish the frequency of the asserted systematic reasoning errors.

The symmetry results are encouraging but do not establish the claimed inherent 3D understanding. Correlated silhouettes, visible face patterns, and shape-family cues remain possible explanations. There are no controls for these shortcuts, uncertainty estimates across held-out shapes, or convincing justification for excluding Johnson solids because of viewpoint ambiguity.

Technical inaccuracies weaken confidence in a benchmark whose value depends on precise geometry: Section 3.2 incorrectly attributes edge transitivity to Archimedean solids generally and describes Catalan solids as retaining vertex uniformity. Claims that difficult distinctions are readily apparent to humans are unsupported by a human evaluation. Overall, the resource has potential, but the evaluation and documentation require substantial revision to meet a top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: GIQ addresses a relevant gap: evaluating precise geometric properties using polyhedra with well-defined structure, rather than relying only on heterogeneous everyday objects.

The collection of synthetic renderings and carefully constructed physical paper models is a valuable contribution. Diverse polyhedral families, viewpoints, and indoor/outdoor conditions offer useful opportunities for controlled evaluation.

The symmetry experiment provides concrete positive evidence: probes trained on synthetic images generalize to 26 unseen shapes, with DINOv2 achieving wild-image balanced accuracies of 0.85 and 0.93 for five-fold and four-fold rotation, respectively.

Evaluating reconstruction, symmetry prediction, shape matching, and VLM recognition across multiple models gives the benchmark useful breadth. The qualitative examples clearly illustrate potentially informative failure modes.
weaknesses: The reconstruction claims substantially exceed the quantitative evidence. Section 4.1 presents selected outputs for three shapes under synthetic and real conditions, without dataset-wide geometric metrics, uncertainty estimates, or analysis against shape complexity. These examples demonstrate failures but cannot establish their prevalence or support broad comparisons between reconstruction methods.

The main mental-rotation result has a problematic metric interpretation. Figure 2 explicitly reports accuracy on negative pairs only, which measures specificity rather than overall same/different discrimination. An always-different predictor would score 100% on this subset. Consequently, proximity to the plotted 50% line does not establish chance-level task performance without positive-pair results, balanced accuracy, and threshold details.

The tasks do not sufficiently isolate geometric reasoning. Synthetic–wild matching changes appearance, background, and imaging conditions alongside viewpoint; absolute-difference embeddings with a linear probe test one restricted readout. Likewise, naming obscure polyhedra confounds visual understanding with specialist vocabulary and prior knowledge. Controlled appearance experiments, direct geometric-property questions, stronger matching baselines, and human performance would strengthen the interpretation.

The zero-shot classification protocol is insufficiently specified: evaluated image counts, viewpoint selection, handling of alternative valid names, scoring procedures, model versions, and inference settings are missing. The Gemini example refers to Google search, leaving tool access and comparability unclear. Selected failure narratives do not establish the frequency of the claimed systematic reasoning errors.

Benchmark reproducibility and composition require clarification. The supplied PDF refers essential splits, ablations, and results to supplementary material that is not included, and its public-release 'here' text provides no usable link. Claims of 224 real polyhedra are difficult to reconcile with Section 3.4's narrower physical collection, including only 48 of the 92 Johnson solids. Exact inventories, category overlaps, annotations, and per-task sample counts are needed.

The symmetry results are promising but lack repeated shape-level splits, confidence intervals, and controls for correlated visible features or polyhedral families. Excluding Johnson solids also narrows the evaluation substantially. Predictability of symmetry labels supports useful representation content, but does not by itself establish intrinsic 3D reasoning.

Several geometric descriptions need correction, particularly because precise geometry is the benchmark's foundation. Section 3.2 incorrectly describes Archimedean solids as retaining edge-transitivity and describes Catalan solids as retaining vertex uniformity, contradicting their generally non-vertex-transitive nature and the paper's own table.

strengths: GIQ targets a useful evaluation gap: fine-grained geometric understanding of polyhedra with known structure and symmetry. Combining synthetic renderings with photographed physical models is a valuable and labor-intensive contribution.
The evaluation spans reconstruction, symmetry prediction, mental rotation, and shape naming, covering diverse image encoders, frontier VLMs, and geometry-oriented models.

The symmetry experiment uses shape-disjoint five-fold cross-validation and balanced accuracy. DINOv2’s reported approximately 93% balanced accuracy on real-image 4-fold symmetry detection after synthetic-only training is a concrete positive finding.
The 42-participant human study provides useful context for the difficulty of distinguishing similar polyhedra.
weaknesses: Essential evidence is unavailable in the supplied manuscript. Numerous quantitative results, probe configurations, dataset details, and CoT/multiview ablations are deferred to an appendix, but the PDF ends with references. Exact evaluation sample counts, model configurations, optimization settings, and uncertainty estimates are inadequately documented, preventing reproducibility and verification of several central claims.

Reconstruction conclusions substantially exceed the presented evidence. Table 1 provides selected qualitative examples without aggregate reconstruction metrics, geometric constraint measurements, alignment procedures, or a systematic complexity analysis. Its caption describes three synthetic/real shape pairs, while the displayed table contains only four input rows. These examples establish failures, but not their prevalence across GIQ.

The mental rotation evaluation confounds geometric discrimination with synthetic-to-real domain shift. Hard-pair selection, class balance, and train/test separation by shape, image, and pair are insufficiently specified. The claimed synthetic-only controls are unavailable, and simple similarity or matching baselines are missing. Consequently, the performance drop cannot be cleanly attributed to deficient mental rotation.

Open-ended polyhedron naming mixes geometric perception with specialist vocabulary and familiarity. Qualitative property errors are informative, but aggregate naming accuracy does not establish failure of the underlying geometric abilities. Direct property questions and controlled recognition baselines are needed. The assertion that one view is informationally complete for entire high-symmetry categories is unjustified without additional assumptions about visibility and candidate shapes.

The human comparison does not establish a robust human advantage: the best model scores approximately 69%, compared with a human mean of 68.05%. Reporting that 68% of participants outperform the model, or highlighting the best participants, requires uncertainty estimates and a clearly matched item-level comparison, particularly with only 20 hard questions per participant.

Dataset scope and mathematical definitions need correction. Figure 1 describes 224 real polyhedra, whereas Section 3.4 includes only 48 of the 92 Johnson solids, leaving actual real-domain coverage unclear. Section 3.2 incorrectly treats edge-transitivity as a general Archimedean property, and Section 3.1’s regular-polyhedron definition omits the required vertex condition. Such inaccuracies weaken confidence in a benchmark whose key promise is precise geometric ground truth.

The conclusions overgeneralize from a narrow benchmark. Neither low naming accuracy nor single-view reconstruction failures establish that models rely on texture rather than geometry, that scaling is insufficient, or that they are unprepared for complex real-world scenes. The dataset is promising, but the available evidence and experimental controls are insufficient for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: GIQ addresses a relevant evaluation gap through mathematically structured polyhedra, combining synthetic renderings, physical paper models, and corresponding meshes. The collection of 224 distinct shapes could become a useful diagnostic resource.

The symmetry experiment uses shape-disjoint five-fold cross-validation, balanced accuracy, and synthetic-to-real transfer. DINOv2’s approximately 93% balanced accuracy for four-fold symmetry provides a concrete positive finding.

The evaluation covers several complementary tasks and diverse model families, including geometry-pretrained models. The 42-participant human study and manual checking of naming synonyms are useful additions.
weaknesses: Essential evidence is unavailable in the supplied manuscript. The 14-page PDF ends with references, although quantitative reconstruction results, synthetic-domain results, probe comparisons, prompting and multiview ablations, and dataset details are repeatedly deferred to an appendix. Consequently, important claims cannot be checked, and the experimental protocols are insufficiently reproducible.

The tasks do not adequately isolate geometric reasoning. Open-ended polyhedron naming requires specialized terminology and factual knowledge, while synthetic-to-real matching also measures appearance and domain robustness. Poor performance therefore does not establish the claimed fundamental architectural deficiency. Direct property questions, controlled appearance changes, and quantitative same-domain versus cross-domain comparisons would help distinguish these explanations.

The reconstruction evidence is primarily selected qualitative examples. Section 4.1 provides no aggregate geometric metrics, uncertainty estimates, or systematic analysis across complexity levels. Table 1 also displays four input rows despite describing synthetic/real pairs for three shapes. This evidence is insufficient to substantiate broad claims about reconstruction reliability across the benchmark.

The mental-rotation protocol is underspecified: the hard-pair selection procedure, sample counts, class balance, probe architecture, and separation of shapes and images across training and testing are unclear. Unlike the symmetry experiment, shape-disjoint evaluation is not explicitly established. The best model approximately matches the human mean, so emphasizing that 68% of participants outperform it does not by itself demonstrate a reliable human–model gap; matched-item comparisons and uncertainty estimates are needed.

Benchmark composition and experimental controls need clarification. Figure 1 describes 224 real polyhedra, whereas Section 3.4 includes only 48 of the 92 Johnson solids and does not reconcile the real-object total. Exact per-task counts and annotation validation are missing. For frontier models, inference settings, repeated trials, and tool access are unspecified; Figure 4 includes a Gemini response reporting a Google search.

Several mathematical statements are incorrect or insufficiently justified. Archimedean solids are not generally edge-transitive, congruent regular faces alone do not define a regular polyhedron, and the introduction incorrectly calls the tetrahedron Archimedean. The assertion that a single view is informationally complete for high-symmetry categories is also not established. These issues matter because precise geometric definitions and ground truth are central to the benchmark’s value.

The conclusions exceed the demonstrated findings. Failure on specialized polyhedra does not establish texture-based reasoning, show that scaling is insufficient, or imply inability to handle complex scenes and dynamics. The resource is promising, but the missing validation and unresolved confounds leave the submission below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: GIQ targets a useful evaluation gap: controlled assessment of geometric properties using mathematically structured objects. Combining synthetic renderings with photographs of physical polyhedra is a promising and labor-intensive dataset contribution.
The evaluation spans reconstruction, symmetry detection, mental rotation, and shape classification, covering diverse visual encoders, frontier VLMs, and geometry-oriented models.

The symmetry experiment uses shape-disjoint five-fold cross-validation and balanced accuracy. DINOv2’s reported 93% balanced accuracy for four-fold symmetry on real photographs after synthetic-only training is an interesting positive finding.
The 42-participant human study provides useful context for task difficulty, and the paper acknowledges that its strongest mental-rotation model approximately matches average human performance.
weaknesses: Essential supporting evidence is absent from the supplied manuscript. The 14-page PDF ends with references, although it repeatedly delegates quantitative reconstruction results, synthetic-domain results, probe comparisons, hard-pair examples, and CoT/multiview ablations to an appendix. Consequently, several central claims cannot be verified.

The reconstruction evidence shown is qualitative and limited to three selected shapes. There are no reported aggregate geometric metrics, uncertainty estimates, or systematic measurements of symmetry, face planarity, topology, or complexity-dependent degradation. These examples do not substantiate the broad claim that reconstruction methods generally fail even on basic Platonic solids.

The tasks do not adequately isolate geometric reasoning. Open-ended polyhedron naming confounds geometric perception with knowledge of specialized nomenclature; poor performance even with ground-truth point clouds does not resolve that confound. The mental-rotation experiment simultaneously introduces difficult negative pairs and a synthetic-to-real domain shift. Direct property questions and controlled comparisons across domain, viewpoint, and pair difficulty are needed.

Evaluation protocols are insufficiently specified for reproduction. Missing details include hard-pair selection, pair counts and balance, whether MRT splits prevent shape or image overlap, probe architecture and optimization, feature extraction choices, and VLM inference settings. Figure 4 includes a response claiming Google search use, but tool access and its consistency across models are unexplained. Reported model differences lack confidence intervals.

Dataset documentation needs reconciliation and validation. Figure 1 describes 224 real polyhedra, whereas Section 3.4 lists only 48 of the 92 Johnson solids without explaining the resulting real-image inventory. Exact image counts, mesh provenance, and annotation verification are unclear. Geometric definitions also contain errors: congruent regular faces alone do not establish regularity, and Archimedean solids are not generally edge-transitive.

The conclusions substantially exceed the evidence. A single view is not generally informationally complete merely because an object is highly symmetric. Naming failures and domain-shift errors do not establish a fundamental architectural deficit or prove that representations are texture-based. Likewise, average-human parity on MRT, with only 20 hard questions per participant and no paired uncertainty analysis, does not establish the claimed robust human advantage. The dataset has potential, but the current evidence and documentation are insufficient for acceptance at a selective conference.
